tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__add_repo
tools.description:
Add a GitHub repository to the current session so you can read, clone, or operate on it alongside the repos already in the session. Call this whenever you need a repository the session does not have — including when someone only asks a question about one, rather than asking for it to be attached. Prefer attaching a repository over reporting that you cannot reach it. 

IMPORTANT — DO NOT PRE-CHECK THE REPO BEFORE CALLING THIS TOOL. Do not curl github.com, do not run `gh repo view`, do not run `git ls-remote` to verify the repo exists. Unauthenticated requests to private repos return 404 ("Not Found") even when the repo is real and your session has authorized access to it. Those preemptive 404s will mislead you into skipping the tool. Instead: call add_repo with the owner/repo exactly as you have it. The backend performs the real reachability + authorization check and returns a structured error you can act on. If the repo genuinely doesn't exist or isn't accessible, the tool response will tell you — report that to the user. If it does exist, the tool response will include a clone command you can then run. Do not report success until the tool has actually been called and returned. 

WHEN ACCESS IS DENIED: if the tool returns an authorization or policy error — the repo exists but isn't enabled for this workspace/project/organization, or the GitHub App isn't installed or linked — relay the tool's exact reason to the user. The response names the remedy: if Claude doesn't have GitHub access for this organization at all, the user should reconnect GitHub under claude.ai Settings → Connectors; if the repo is simply not in the allowed set, a Claude.ai organization owner can grant access in the settings page the response points to. Do not add settings URLs beyond those provided here or in the tool response. Do not retry the same repo. You may remind the user which repositories are already available in this session, and offer to help them request access. Do not guess, infer, or list repositories you cannot see in the tool res… [truncated]

access.description: What access this session needs. "read" (default): fetch/clone only — when the repository is public, git read access is often already served by the session's git proxy with nothing to attach, and the tool says so instead of attaching. repo.description: GitHub repo name, e.g. "claude-code". Do not include the owner prefix — pass owner and repo as separate fields.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__create_session
tools.description: Create a new Claude Code Remote session. Returns the new session's ID and status. If environment_id is omitted, the new session inherits the calling session's environment. Combine with send_message for fan-out orchestration: spawn a sibling and send it a task. Where enabled, this session receives a <child-session-event> turn if the new session's turn fails or its worker restarts and drops background tasks; a session that finishes cleanly does not report back, so check on it with get_session (status_bucket reads 'failed' for a turn that errored, where status alone reads 'idle' either way) and list_events.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__create_session
schema.description: Create a new Claude Code Remote session. Returns the new session's ID and status. If environment_id is omitted, the new session inherits the calling session's environment. Combine with send_message for fan-out orchestration: spawn a sibling and send it a task. Where enabled, this session receives a <child-session-event> turn if the new session's turn fails or its worker restarts and drops background tasks; a session that finishes cleanly does not report back, so check on it with get_session (status_bucket reads 'failed' for a turn that errored, where status alone reads 'idle' either way) and list_events.

append_system_prompt.description: Text appended to the new session's system prompt.

blob_limit_kb.description: Optional. Files larger than this many KB are left out of the checkout; git fetches one on demand when a command reads it. Requires source_url. Set it for very large repositories, whose sessions otherwise fail to start for lack of disk space. Ignored when sparse_checkout_paths is set.

clone_depth.description: Optional number of commits of history to fetch (default 50). Requires source_url. Lower it for very large repositories.

environment_id.description: Environment ID — a tagged ID starting with 'env_' (or 'ccpool_' for self-hosted pools). Defaults to the calling session's environment. Do NOT invent a value — call list_environments to get the user's real environment_ids. When this resolves to the remote_cowork environment (explicitly or via inheritance), a Claude Cowork session is spawned — the account's enabled skills, plugins and the Cowork system prompt are assembled server-side, and only prompt, title, model and tags are read (source_url, extra_allowed_tools, append_system_prompt and environment_variables are ignored so the caller cannot widen the tool surface).

extra_allowed_tools.description: Extra tool names pre-approved without a user permission prompt. Entries the calling session does not itself have pre-approved are dropped — the child never carries a grant its parent lacks.

model.description: Model ID for the new session. Defaults to the calling session's model.

outcome_branch.description: Optional branch name to push changes to. When set, the session pushes directly to this branch (no session-derived suffix appended).

permission_mode.description: Initial permission mode for the new session. Cannot be more permissive than the calling session's mode; omit to inherit it. 'plan' makes the agent propose a plan and then BLOCKS waiting for human approval via the claude.ai/code web UI — do NOT use 'plan' for autonomous child sessions that no human is watching, as they will stall indefinitely at the approval prompt.

prompt.description: Optional initial message to send to the new session.

source_revision.description: Optional git branch, tag, or commit to check out. Requires source_url. Defaults to the repo's default branch.

source_url.description: Optional git repository URL to check out.

sparse_checkout_paths.description: Optional directories, relative to the repository root. The checkout holds only these, plus the files directly in their parent folders and at the root. Requires source_url. Set it to work in part of a very large repository.

tags.description: Free-form tags to categorize the session (e.g. ["remote-agents-project:frontend"]). Editable later via set_session_tags.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__create_trigger
tools.description: Create a Routine (scheduled trigger). Three targeting modes: (1) default — fires into THIS SESSION, resuming the same conversation each time; (2) persistent_session_id set — fires into a SPECIFIC OTHER SESSION you name (must be in your account); (3) create_new_session_on_fire=true — spawns a FRESH SESSION in this environment on each firing. Use mode 1 for recurring work you want to pick back up yourself; mode 2 for waking a sibling session you created; mode 3 when each firing should start from a clean slate. If the result warns that the Routine stores no connectors, say so plainly when you confirm the Routine to the user and pass on the remedy it names; never report such a Routine as simply created.

Use mode 1 for recurring work you want to pick back up yourself; mode 2 for waking a sibling session you created; mode 3 when each firing should start from a clean slate. connectors.description: Optional list of connector names the Routine's fired sessions may use, e.g. ["Gmail", "linear"]. Pass ONLY connectors the user explicitly asked this Routine to use — the stored grant applies to every future firing. Names resolve against the user's connected claude.ai connectors; when calling from inside a CCR session the list is further limited to connectors that session itself holds (it can only narrow that set, never widen it). Any name that cannot be resolved fails the call. Pass [] to store no connectors. Omit to keep the default behavior for this surface. The grant attaches the connectors only — individual tool calls from fired sessions still go through runtime permission checks.

create_new_session_on_fire.description: If true, each firing creates a fresh session in the calling session's environment instead of resuming an existing one. Default false. Mutually exclusive with persistent_session_id.

cron_expression.description: Standard 5-field cron expression (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week). Fields without a prefix are UTC. If you know the user's time zone, write the fields in their local time after CRON_TZ=<IANA time zone> and a space (weekdays at 8:52am in Los Angeles: CRON_TZ=America/Los_Angeles 52 8 * * 1-5). If not, ask. Minimum interval is normally hourly (some projects allow shorter); a too-frequent schedule is rejected and the error names the minimum. For hourly or every-N-hours schedules, use minute 0 (e.g. '0 * * * *', '0 */4 * * *'): the server anchors it to the creation minute ('hourly starting now'), so Routines spread across the hour instead of all firing at :00. All other schedules are stored verbatim. When a recurring schedule (run_once_at is unset) at a fixed time of day would land on the hour or half hour (a plain '9am' or '9:30'), prefer using a jittered minute value instead. Most schedules run on minute 0, so runs scheduled at those times can be delayed due to server traffic. By default, move the time 1 to 15 minutes earlier (for '9am', 8:45 to 8:59); use the number of letters in the task's name, modulo 15, plus 1. Leave midnight, a time on any other minute (e.g. 9:10) and a run that must follow an event as asked. Mutually exclusive with run_once_at. Omit both for a poke-only Routine that never fires on its own schedule.

environment_id.description: Environment ID — a tagged ID starting with 'env_' (or 'ccpool_' for self-hosted pools). Defaults to the calling session's environment. Required when calling from outside a CCR session (no session context to inherit from). Do NOT invent a value — call list_environments to get the user's real environment_ids.

initiation.description: Who wanted this: human_request — a person asked you to set this up now; human_schedule — a schedule a person set (e.g. an earlier firing) told you to; own_followup — your own check-in or follow-up on work you are already doing; own_initiative — you decided on your own that this should exist.

notifications.description: Completion notifications for this Routine. push sends to the owner's phone when a run finishes with something noteworthy; email sends the same summary to their inbox. If omitted, the setting stays unset and the server default applies at fire time. Passing this sets an explicit per-Routine choice, so list every channel you want on ({push:true, email:true} for both; {email:true} alone means email-only, push off). Pass {} to opt out of all channels. Only fresh-session-per-fire Routines (create_new_session_on_fire=true) take this; the server rejects it for self-bind or persistent_session_id Routines.

persistent_session_id.description: Optional session ID to fire into instead of this one. Must belong to the same account — the server rejects sessions you don't own. Omit to fire into this session (default). Mutually exclusive with create_new_session_on_fire.

prompt.description: The message the Routine sends on each firing. When binding to an existing session (modes 1-2), write it assuming past context — the conversation continues. In fresh-session mode (mode 3), write it as a complete standalone instruction since each firing starts from nothing.

run_once_at.description: RFC3339 timestamp for a one-shot fire (e.g. 2026-04-20T17:00:00Z). Must be in the future. Mutually exclusive with cron_expression — set one or the other, not both. After the one-shot fires the Routine disables itself with ended_reason=run_once_fired. Use exactly the time asked: the guidance on recurring schedules does not apply to a one-time run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__delete_trigger
tools.description: Delete a Routine (scheduled trigger). The Routine must belong to the calling session's account — deleting another account's Routine fails with not-found. Use this to undo a create_trigger call or to clean up Routines whose work is done. A bad cron or wrong prompt does not need deletion — update_trigger fixes those in place, keeping the Routine's run history. On success, the result usually echoes the deleted Routine's last state (including its name) in the response's trigger field — callers without stored-data read access get a plain-text confirmation instead. Either way the Routine no longer exists once this returns.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__get_session
tools.description: Get details for a specific Claude Code Remote session by ID. Returns the session's title, status, status_bucket (working / blocked / review_ready / completed / failed — 'failed' means its last turn errored), creation time, and context. Every returned session carries three model fields: configured_model is the model stored at creation, echoed as stored (it may be an alias or carry a context-window suffix, so normalize before comparing); session_context.model is the model the session is currently set to run (the creation-time model, or a later switch or refusal fallback); external_metadata.last_served_model is the model the CLI ran the latest turn on, which also reflects turn-scoped fallbacks (overload or unavailable) that do not change session_context.model. To detect a switch or fallback in a child session, compare configured_model against both session_context.model and external_metadata.last_served_model; the fallback notices in list_events give the reason. Omit session_id to describe this session.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__list_triggers
tools.description: List Routines (scheduled triggers) owned by this account. Use it to find trigger IDs (trig_...) for update_trigger and delete_trigger. From a thread in a Slack channel, only Routines that fire into that thread's session are listed unless all_in_channel is true. Each entry has the Routine's id, name, cron_expression, run_once_at, enabled state, ended_reason, next_run_at, created_at, persistent_session_id, and last_run. last_run is the most recent recorded run {status, fired_at, finished_at, session_id}. It is absent when no run was recorded (e.g. never fired). For a Routine that wakes an existing session, last_run records that the wake was delivered (SUCCEEDED) or failed to deliver, not how the turn went, unless run tracking covers that session. A FAILED or repeatedly non-SUCCEEDED last_run means the Routine is not doing its job. ended_reason says why a disabled Routine is permanently disabled. suspension_reason (e.g. subscription_paused) marks a temporary hold that lifts when the owner's subscription resumes. Both empty means user-paused. One-shot Routines that already fired (e.g. delivered send_later reminders) and Routines moved to a project are hidden unless include_completed is true. Scheduled tasks stored locally by the Cowork desktop app are not listed.

all_in_channel.description: Threads in a Slack channel only. If true, list every Routine in this channel, including other threads' and ones that start a new session each time they fire. Default false.

enabled.description: When set, only Routines whose enabled state matches. true hides fired one-shots, paused, and auto-disabled Routines; false shows only those. Omit for both.

include_completed.description: If true, also include one-shot Routines that have already fired (e.g. delivered send_later reminders) and Routines moved to a project. Default false — there can be thousands.

recurring.description: When set, filters by schedule shape: true keeps only cron-driven (recurring) Routines, false only one-shot and fire-only Routines. Omit for both.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__read_documentation
tools.description: The documentation for the machine and product this session runs in: a claude.ai cloud container and the settings around it (GitHub access, connectors, the environment's secrets, network access, setup script and installed tools, the session's limits, Remote Control). Read it whenever something about your container or environment comes up, whether it blocked you, you worked around it, or the person asked how to set it up. For example: the repository the work is about is not in your container, a clone or push is refused, a service you need has no connected connector, an outbound host is denied, a command-line tool is missing, you need an API key. Read it rather than answering from memory because these settings move and get renamed faster than your training data, and a page says what is true now: the current steps, where in the product the person makes the change, and what you can do yourself. Reading a page also helps the person directly: in the Claude Code app they see a card with a button that takes them to that settings page, so they can fix it themselves while you carry on. Call it with no topic to list the pages and when each applies; call it with a topic to read that page. Read a page each time a different topic comes up; one read per topic is enough. It is read-only and needs no approval. It has nothing on bugs in the code you are working on.

This is a thin wrapper over create_trigger (a self-bind + run_once_at Routine); the returned trigger_id can be passed to delete_trigger to cancel before it fires, and the Routine disables itself after firing once.

Most schedules run on minute 0, so runs scheduled at those times can be delayed due to server traffic. By default, move the time 1 to 15 minutes earlier (for '9am', 8:45 to 8:59); use the number of letters in the task's name, modulo 15, plus 1. <?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. ## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

"Passages not yet revised" says the question is open (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1556-1560`). Pavol's decision of 2026-09-27, a size's range (POSITIONS.md): "A `nat` parameter is an `NN32` value and an `int` parameter a `ZZ32` (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:82-90`); a larger one is refused". ### 1. The rule

**Decided: way 2**, reading A of `option-2-soundness.md`: the coercion chapter's order over declarations, with applicability and specificity taken on declared, quantified domains as answer 9 words them, and answer 8's promotion as the instantiation of the selected declaration, its coercions inserted statically and the rewritten call dispatching on the converted values.

**Stated for the specification** (rung T's inference chapter; batch 7b's rung S for the coercion chapter's cross-reference):

> *Resolution* (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:472-476`, `:533-553`, unchanged in substance). For a static call `f(A)` or `A₀.f(A)`, let Σ be the declarations of `f` applicable to the call without coercion, a declaration with static parameters being applicable when some instance within its bounds is (`Papers/Types/setup.tick:393-397`; answer 9), and compared on those quantified domains. If Σ is not empty, its most specific declaration is selected. Otherwise, among the declarations applicable with coercion, the one whose parameter type is no less specific (`⪯`, `:486-513`) than every other's is selected; the overloading rules guarantee that it exists and is unique, and where they do not, the call is a static error.
>
> *Instantiation* (the inference chapter). The static arguments of the selected declaration are then inferred: a static parameter takes the narrowest type, under `⪯`, that every argument constraining it is substitutable for (`:417-432`), its bounds permitting; for number arguments this is the narrowest type every one of them converts into (answer 8). The coercions this instance needs are inserted into the call statically, like any coercion resolved statically (`:584-591`).
>
> *Dispatch* (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:262-276`). The rewritten call dispatches at run time, by subtyping and without further coercion, to the most specific declaration applicable to the converted values.
>
> *Numerals* (Q1; decision 4 below). Where a numeral's candidate types are incomparable under `⪯`, in either step, the numeral is read as `ZZ32`, or as `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit.

**Reasons.**
- One principle at two levels, not two rules. A conversion makes a call possible and never changes which body runs when a body already fits (`conversions-coercions.tex:279-282`, `:472-476`). Answer 8 chooses among instances of one body; it never chooses between bodies. So the designers' order and answer 8 do not conflict once applicability is read on declared domains, which answer 9 already decided (`reviews/overloading-judgement.md` section 3.4: "inference instantiates the chosen declaration; it does not precede the comparison").
- Sound, with one sentence. `option-2-soundness.md` section 1: the Meet Rule, the uniqueness facts and the appendix lemma speak of declared domains, which reading A does not change (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:247-274`, `:449-470`; `Specification/appendices/overloading-coercion.tex:75-96`). Section 2: the converted call's re-dispatch to `plain64` is type-safe by the return-type rule over every instance (measured, `O2Z64` on the rule and opt2 builds). Section 3: the Meet Rule does its job (`O2Meet`, every build). Section 4: it is answer 9's own order.
- The designers' record is unanimous for this order, and the type group's later word does not contradict it. The coercion chapter (2007-2009; `0f49d8698`). The checker's coercion-first ranking (Hilburn, 2009-08-18, `fc99e1ef2`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1085-1095`, opened and read). The compiled library, whose `=` and `=/=` are per type with no arm over `Any` or `Number` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:123-124`, `:167-168`, `:229-230`, `:299-300`, `:359-360`, `:412-413`, `:445`), general equality being `Equality[\T\] comprises T` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi:24-26`), so that under this order `z = 0` reaches `ZZ32`'s own `=` with the numeral converted: by reading, Σ is empty, and `(ZZ32, ZZ32) ⪯ (ZZ64, ZZ64)` and `⪯ (ZZ, ZZ)` because `IntLiteral`, the one type that converts into `ZZ32`, excludes both (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:390`). The 2011 paper and Welterweight have no coercion (`Papers/Types/rules.tick:118-129`; `Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:67`, `:187-193`). Protocol principle 1 and POSITIONS 2026-09-23 give the later word more weight where the two conflict; here nothing conflicts.
- The peers. Java (strict invocation before loose), C++ (an exact match beats a promotion beats a conversion, and a user-defined conversion ranks lowest), Swift (a score that counts conversions first) and Julia (never converts in dispatch; the library's catch-alls promote) all put an unconverted arm first; C# alone ranks by the conversion's target (`conversion-overloading-ways.md` section 6). ts: it infers
the static arguments of a declaration with static parameters with coercion,
and instantiates the declaration that its dispatch chooses by the rule for a
type parameter that is a parameter's whole type.
So where the declared type of a variable is wider than the type of its value,
or an argument's static type is \TYP{Any}, it may run a declaration at a
narrower instance than the compiled path, which instantiates it at the static
types.
It does not yet fix a type parameter by the expected type, compare
declarations with static parameters on the parameter types they declare, nor
dispatch a converted call again.}

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
number types (\secref{literals}).
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
value does not fit in the narrower type.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values.

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
is a static error.

This chapter does not yet describe:
\begin{itemize}
\item the static arguments of a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator
parameter (\secref{boolparams}, \secref{dimunitparams}, \secref{opr-ident});
\item a static parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes,
such as a type parameter that only the return type mentions, as its whole type,
or the element type of a reduction that only its generator clauses determine
(\secref{reduction-expr}); whether inference may give such a parameter
\TYP{BottomType}, which programmers must not write (\secref{bottom-type}), is
left open;
\item whether an argument whose declared parameter type mentions a static
parameter inside another type may be converted where only a conversion of its
elements would satisfy the bounds of the parameter; under the rule above such
an argument fixes the parameter by subtyping and is not converted;
\item an expected type in any context other than those listed above, such as
an argument of another call, an expression that a local declaration precedes in
a block, an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, a \KWD{typecase}
expression, the body of a \KWD{for} loop, or a call written by loose
juxtaposition, as \EXP{f\;x};
\item the static arguments of an object with static parameters that is named
without a call, which a program writes (\secref{where-clauses});
\item the inference over a whole program of the types that declarations elide
(\secref{type-inference-components}).
\end{itemize}
\revision{revival-inference}{For a type parameter that only the return type
mentions, the compiled type checker binds the parameter to \TYP{BottomType},
except that it refuses a call that has no expected type when the parameter is
declared \EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}; the interpreter erases such a parameter
to \TYP{BottomType} (rows~424, 425 and~447 of the revival's gap ledger).
Whether inference may do so is the team's question, kept in the draft note
below.
Neither implementation infers a \KWD{bool} parameter yet: the compiled type
checker refuses by name to infer a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim} or \KWD{unit}
parameter, and the interpreter does not unify a \KWD{bool} one (rows~21
and~307 of the revival's gap ledger).
The example of \secref{boolparams}, a coercion whose \KWD{bool} parameter only
its parameter type mentions, can be applied only if its argument fixes that
parameter.}

\note{ \begin{itemize}
 \item
 There seems to be a circular dependency between inference and juxtaposition
 disambiguation -- you have to know if the subexpressions have arrow types
 to disambiguate, but you can't do that without using inference, which
 requires knowing how the variable of unknown type is used.
\item Type Inference (Dan's email titled ``Comments on a first reading of the spec'' on 06/05/07)
\item Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers
\TYP{BottomType}s for static parameters?
 \end{itemize}
}

ts: it infers
the static arguments of a declaration with static parameters with coercion,
and instantiates the declaration that its dispatch chooses by the rule for a
type parameter that is a parameter's whole type.
So where the declared type of a variable is wider than the type of its value,
or an argument's static type is \TYP{Any}, it may run a declaration at a
narrower instance than the compiled path, which instantiates it at the static
types.
It does not yet fix a type parameter by the expected type, compare
declarations with static parameters on the parameter types they declare, nor
dispatch a converted call again.}

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
number types (\secref{literals}).
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
value does not fit in the narrower type.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values.

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
is a static error.

This chapter does not yet describe:
\begin{itemize}
\item the static arguments of a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator
parameter (\secref{boolparams}, \secref{dimunitparams}, \secref{opr-ident});
\item a static parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes,
such as a type parameter that only the return type mentions, as its whole type,
or the element type of a reduction that only its generator clauses determine
(\secref{reduction-expr}); whether inference may give such a parameter
\TYP{BottomType}, which programmers must not write (\secref{bottom-type}), is
left open;
\item whether an argument whose declared parameter type mentions a static
parameter inside another type may be converted where only a conversion of its
elements would satisfy the bounds of the parameter; under the rule above such
an argument fixes the parameter by subtyping and is not converted;
\item an expected type in any context other than those listed above, such as
an argument of another call, an expression that a local declaration precedes in
a block, an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, a \KWD{typecase}
expression, the body of a \KWD{for} loop, or a call written by loose
juxtaposition, as \EXP{f\;x};
\item the static arguments of an object with static parameters that is named
without a call, which a program writes (\secref{where-clauses});
\item the inference over a whole program of the types that declarations elide
(\secref{type-inference-components}).
\end{itemize}
\revision{revival-inference}{For a type parameter that only the return type
mentions, the compiled type checker binds the parameter to \TYP{BottomType},
except that it refuses a call that has no expected type when the parameter is
declared \EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}; the interpreter erases such a parameter
to \TYP{BottomType} (rows~424, 425 and~447 of the revival's gap ledger).
Whether inference may do so is the team's question, kept in the draft note
below.
Neither implementation infers a \KWD{bool} parameter yet: the compiled type
checker refuses by name to infer a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim} or \KWD{unit}
parameter, and the interpreter does not unify a \KWD{bool} one (rows~21
and~307 of the revival's gap ledger).
The example of \secref{boolparams}, a coercion whose \KWD{bool} parameter only
its parameter type mentions, can be applied only if its argument fixes that
parameter.}

\note{ \begin{itemize}
 \item
 There seems to be a circular dependency between inference and juxtaposition
 disambiguation -- you have to know if the subexpressions have arrow types
 to disambiguate, but you can't do that without using inference, which
 requires knowing how the variable of unknown type is used.
\item Type Inference (Dan's email titled ``Comments on a first reading of the spec'' on 06/05/07)
\item Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers
\TYP{BottomType}s for static parameters?
 \end{itemize}
}

content.content:
## 7. What the rule does not reach, and the forks it meets

Each item is measured where it names a capture, read otherwise.

- **Numerals alone at a bound a numeral does not meet, on A0.** `lohi(2, 46)` with `I extends AnyIntegral`, `twice(3, 4)` with `T extends Integral[\T\]`, `(): ZZ64 = inc(5)`, and today's generic ranges `2:46`, `0#3`, `0#vs` are refused stock and under the rule (`small/RuleL.outcomes-any.txt`, `small/DArg.summary-any.txt`), and so are microGPT's four ranges of the shape (section 3) and the library's three (section 4). The lone parameter's choices are its arguments' type, `IntLiteral`, and its bound when that is a plain trait type (`AnyIntegral`, which a numeral does not convert into; an F-bound is skipped), and none succeeds. Today they pass on L0 only because `IntLiteral extends ZZ32` there. The ways the language offers, none decided here:
  1. the ranges batch before batch N (the recorded order): `#` and `:` over `ZZ32` are not generic, so a numeral converts at them as at any call; section 3's A0T2 measures that on microGPT;
  2. the expected type as one more choice when the result is the lone parameter, so that `(): ZZ64 = inc(5)` and `x: ZZ64 = twice(3, 4)` infer `ZZ64` [not built];
  3. a default type for a numeral that nothing else fixes, among its coercion targets that meet the bound, as Java's `int`, Rust's `i32` fallback and Haskell's defaulting do; `ZZ32` and `NN32` both convert from a numeral and neither into the other, so "the narrowest" does not pick one, and the specification writes no default (`literals.tex:83-95`, the unfinished numeral hierarchy), so it would be a decision;
  4. the written static argument, today's device and answer 8's interim rule.
- **A narrowest common type that is neither argument's.** `ZZ32` with `NN32`: `pick(u, z)`, `lohi(z, u)` and `seq(z:u)` keep the union `OR(ZZ32,NN32)`, where answer 8's rule names `ZZ64`, the narrowest type both convert into (`small/RuleL.outcomes-any.txt`, `small/OneShapeW.summary-any.txt`). Finding it needs, for each argument type, the types that declare a coercion from it; the checker's oracle only goes from a target to its sources (`getCoercionsTo`, `scala_src/typechecker/CoercionOracle.scala:85-115`), and the trait table can be iterated (`TraitTable.scala:99-110`) to build the reverse index [read, not built]. Neither the library's distance nor microGPT's own errors move with the promotion (sections 3 and 4), so no error there comes from this shape today.
- **A structured position.** `SUM <|1, 2, 3|>` (row 432): the list's `IntLiteral` fixes `T` through `Generator[\T\]` and fails the bound `AdditiveGroup[\T\]`; the rule chooses only for a lone parameter and converts only at a lone or non-generic parameter, so it stays refused (`small/OneShapeW.summary-any.txt`).
- **A result-only parameter.** As in measurement D, the kept context binds it to `BottomType` (`DCtx`'s eleven, the natives' shape); the rule does not change that, and what code generation makes of it is measurement D's open question.
- **The other drops of the expected type** (measurement D § 1.3: a loose juxtaposition, an argument, a `let` body, an `if` with no `else`, `typecase`, a `for` body): not changed.
- **The order of the attempts** is this probe's choice: the expected type first, so where it and coercion fix a parameter (`a: BoxT[\ZZ64\] = wrapT(3)`) the call converts its argument, and where they do not (`a: ZZ64 = idt(3)`) the binding converts the result as today. The other order, today's inference first and the context only when it fails, was not built.
- **Messages.** A call written `f(x)` that no attempt accepts, and whose result the binding would refuse, now reports the call's refusal instead of the binding's: 3 sites per setting and library in the probes (2.1), none in the compiler tests (section 5).
- **The comparison of a `case` expression** is checked with the expected type `Boolean` and no check after it (`Functionals.scala:856`); since an attempt without the expected type is kept only when the result converts to it, a non-`Boolean` comparison is not newly accepted [read].
- **A numeral at a non-generic overloaded call on A0.** `w: ZZ64 = widen(4)` is refused, "Right-hand side has type NN64", because A0's numeral picks `widen`'s `NN32` arm; stock and rule alike, 27 sites in `OneShapeW` and 1 in `RuleL` on A0 (`small/OneShapeW.instr.any.A0.txt`). A matter for the library rung of the switch, not for the rule.
- **Code generation.** The calls the rule accepts compiled and ran (2.3, 2.4), and the compiler library's five components compile under the rule (`comp/libcache-rule.txt`); nothing more was probed.
## 1. The edit

`rule.patch`, made by `make-shadow.py` (variant `rule`) and applied to the tree by `git apply` from the repository root (`build.txt` records that it applies). Two files of the compiled checker, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/`:

- `Operators.scala`: measurement D's four one-token edits, `, expected` at `:85`, `:90`, `:197` and `:345`, so that a call written `f(x)` is checked with the type its context expects.
- `Functionals.scala`: 124 lines added and 5 removed (`git apply --numstat`), 21 of the added lines comments. Three pieces.
  - The attempts, in `checkApplication` (`:449` today). The candidates of a call are tried up to four times, and the first attempt in which one is applicable is kept: by subtyping with the expected type (today's inference, now with the context at `f(x)` too); with coercion and the expected type; and, only when there is an expected type, by subtyping without it and with coercion without it. An attempt without the expected type is kept only when the most specific candidate's result is a subtype of the expected type or converts to it (`coercions.substitutableFor`), which is what the retry is for: a typed binding's coercion of the result still applies. The third attempt is today's check of a call `f(x)`, so a call whose result today's binding accepts is accepted again there at the latest. A refused call reports the first attempt's errors. `checkApplicable` and `checkApplicableWithInference` gain a `coerce` switch, default `false`.
  - The first build kept the retry without the expected type whatever the result; on the compiler tests it changed the message of one expected-failure test that pins the text, `XXX6bu`'s `compile_err_equals` (a method invocation refused today by its context, then by the assignment), so the condition was added and the rule's side of every run was repeated; that first run's capture was replaced by the repeat, and the commit message of `b15201e5b` records it.
  - The coercion attempt, a new method `checkApplicableWithCoercion`. The argument positions are sorted by their declared parameter type: a type parameter alone (`x: T`), a type that mentions a static parameter (`b: Box[\T\]`, `base: M[\r, c\]`), or a type that mentions none (`m: ZZ32`). Only the second kind and the expected type constrain the solver, by subtyping as today (the constraint is built with `inferStaticParamsHelper`, the solver the tree already uses). A type parameter that stands alone at some position and appears in no other parameter type is chosen instead: each of "whatever the rest fixes", its own arguments' types and its declared bound (a trait type other than `Object`) is tried, and among those that succeed the narrowest is kept, narrowest meaning substitutable, a subtype or a coercion, for every other success. Then every argument is admitted against the instantiated parameter type by subtyping or by a coercion, which is built into the call as `checkApplicableWithoutInference` builds it for a non-generic call.
  - The promotion case, at the end of `checkApplicableWithInference`: when today's inference succeeds but binds such a lone parameter to a union (`OR(ZZ32,ZZ64)`), the coercion attempt runs with the union's members as the only choices, and its result replaces the union when one member is the narrowest; otherwise the union stays.
- Not changed: the solver (`Formula.scala`), the coercion oracle, the other places that drop the expected type (measurement D § 1.3: a loose juxtaposition, an argument, a `let` body, an `if` with no `else`, `typecase`, a `for` body), and a result-only parameter, which the kept context still binds to `BottomType` as in measurement D.
- The trace used on the small programs is a separate variant (`rule-instr`, `instr` for the tree), off unless `-Dprobe.showInfer=true`; the trace-free `rule` gives the same errors (`small/RuleL.rule.walk.L0.txt`, `small/DArg.rule.walk.L0.txt` against their `rule-instr` captures).

# Rung T (`rung-spec-inference`): the judge's ruling on the skeptic's refusal

Written 2026-09-29 by the batch's judge, on `wip/rung-spec-inference` at `fc7b5a8e7` (the worker's five commits `bcd9f07df..5cc3e32f0` and the skeptic's `fc7b5a8e7`), base `bce66f1fa`. ## 1. Ruling

**Decision: repair.** The rung's approach is right and stays: the chapter in the S1 form, the choice of a declaration before its instantiation, the numeral tie once, the ranges sentence, the Appendix I entry, the re-anchoring, the builds. The skeptic is right that four statements of the new text are false against runs on the base (F1 to F4) and that the record's lines repeat two of them; one of the four (F1) meets the stop the batch record reserves for T, "normative text stating more than rung I builds". ## 2. What the specification and the decisions settle here

- The chapter is to state the rule "as far as rung I builds it and no further" (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-N.md`, section 3, T, "What it writes"), and "normative text stating more than rung I builds (the chapter) or than both paths run today (the ranges sentence)" is a stop reserved for Pavol (the same section, "Stops"), reversible (POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-27, on the stops a batch record reserves for him).

The chapter's Choice paragraph (`Specification/basic/inference.tex:58-67`) and its expected-type paragraph (`:116-122`) state this, and `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:472-476` says the same for a declaration applicable without coercion.     10	%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
    11	
    12	\chapter{Type Inference}
    13	\chaplabel{type-inference}
    14	
    15	A call of a function, a method or an operator whose declaration has static
    16	parameters, or of the constructor of an object that has static parameters,
    17	need not write its static arguments, and most calls do not
    18	(\secref{idn-ref}, \secref{dotted-method-calls}).
    19	The static arguments of a call that does not write them are inferred
    20	statically.
    21	This chapter describes that inference for type parameters (\secref{type-param})
    22	and for \KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters (\secref{natparams}); the inference
    23	of the static arguments of other kinds of static parameter, and the inference
    24	over a whole program of the types that declarations elide
    25	(\secref{type-inference-components}), are not yet described.
    26	\revision{revival-inference}{The Working Draft of February 2011 left this
    27	chapter a heading and two draft notes, the second of which is kept at its end,
    28	although \chapref{multiple-dispatch}, \secref{idn-ref} and
    29	\secref{dotted-method-calls} cite it.
    30	The rule this chapter states is the one the revival decided on 26, 27 and
    31	28~September 2026 and built into the compiled type checker with this text; the
    32	Working Draft had no counterpart to the rule for a numeral whose conversions tie
    33	(\secref{numeral-default}).
    34	It assumes that a type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause is
    35	bounded by \TYP{Any}, as \library\ and the interpreter take it, where
    36	\secref{type-param} says \TYP{Object}, as the compiled path still takes it for
    37	a program's own declarations (row~412 of the revival's gap ledger).
    38	\chapref{multiple-dispatch} still says that static parameters are inferred
    39	before the applicability of a declaration is checked and before declarations
    40	are compared (\secref{functional-applicability},
    41	\secref{dotted-method-applicability}, \secref{resolving-overloading}), where
    42	this chapter chooses a declaration first.
    43	Those sentences, the implicit bound of \secref{type-param}, and the rule of
    44	\chapref{overloaded-declarations} that a functional whose single parameter has
    45	as its type a naked type parameter of bound \TYP{Any} cannot be overloaded,
    46	which under that bound would forbid overloading any functional whose single
    47	parameter's type is a type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause,
    48	are to be revised together, in the revision of the overloading chapters that
    49	the revival decided on 26~September 2026.
    50	The team's later Types chapter gives the coercion relation and the valid
    51	instantiations of a quantified type, and says nothing of inference.}
    52	
    53	\section{The Static Arguments of a Call}
    54	\seclabel{static-arg-inference}
    55	
    56	The static arguments of a call that does not write them are found in two
    57	steps: the declaration that the call invokes is chosen first, and it is
    58	instantiated second.
    59	
    60	\emph{Choice.}
    61	The declaration is chosen as \secref{resolving-coercion} describes.
    62	A declaration with static parameters is applicable to a call, without or with
    63	coercion, if some instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their bounds is
    64	applicable to the call.
    65	Declarations are compared on the parameter types they declare, a declaration
    66	with static parameters on its parameter types taken over every instance that
    67	its bounds allow, and not on an instance inferred for the call.
    68	So a coercion is applied only to make a call possible: it never changes which
    69	declaration is chosen when one is applicable to the call without it.
    70	
    71	\emph{Instantiation.}
    72	The static arguments of the chosen declaration are then inferred, and with them
    73	the instance of the declaration that the call invokes:
    74	\begin{itemize}
    75	\item A type parameter, or a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter, that the
    76	declared type of a parameter mentions other than as the whole type, as
    77	\EXP{b\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} mentions \VAR{T}, is fixed by
    78	the argument at that position, whose type must be a subtype of the parameter
    79	type of the instance.
    80	\item Where the call has an expected type (below), a type parameter that the
    81	declared return type mentions other than as the whole type is fixed by the
    82	expected type as well.
    83	\item A type parameter that is the whole declared type of one or more
    84	parameters, as \VAR{T} is of \EXP{x\COLON{}T}, and that is not fixed as above,
    85	takes, among the types of the arguments at those positions and the types to
    86	which they can be coerced, the narrowest under $\morespecificeq$
    87	(\secref{resolving-coercion}) that every one of those arguments is
    88	substitutable for (\secref{applicability-with-coercion}) and that the bounds of
    89	the type parameter permit.
    90	For number arguments this is the narrowest type into which every one of them
    91	converts: \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and a
    92	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and also for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and an
    93	\EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, though neither of them is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
    94	(\secref{basic-integers}).
    95	Where there is no such narrowest type, and the rule for numerals
    96	(\secref{numeral-default}) does not settle the tie, the type parameter takes
    97	the union of the types of those arguments (\secref{internal-types}), if its
    98	bounds permit that, and none of those arguments is converted.
    99	\item Every argument is then admitted against the corresponding parameter type
   100	of the instance by substitutability: an argument whose type is a subtype of it
   101	is passed as it is, and any other argument is coerced to it
   102	(\secref{coercion}), as an argument is coerced to the declared type of a
   103	parameter of a declaration without static parameters.
   104	\end{itemize}
   105	The coercions that the instance needs are inserted into the call statically,
   106	as is any coercion that \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses.
   107	
   108	\emph{The expected type.}
   109	A call has an expected type in these contexts: as the right-hand side of a
   110	variable or field declaration that declares its type, that type; as the
   111	right-hand side of an assignment to a variable whose type is declared, that
   112	type; as the body of a functional that declares its return type, that type;
   113	as the last expression of a block that has an expected type, where no local
   114	declaration precedes it in the block, the block's expected type; and as a
   115	branch of an \KWD{if} expression with an \KWD{else} clause that has an
   116	expected type, the expected type of the \KWD{if} expression.
   117	The expected type is used whether the call is written by tight juxtaposition,
   118	as \EXP{f(x)} (\secref{juxtameaning}), or as a method invocation or an operator
   119	application.
   120	The return type of the instance that the steps above find must be a subtype of
   121	the expected type.
   122	If they find no such instance, the static arguments are inferred again without
   123	the expected type, and the call is accepted only if the return type of the instance
   124	then found is a subtype of the expected type or can be coerced to it; in the
   125	second case the result of the call is coerced to the expected type
   126	(\secref{coercion}).
   127	So, for the declarations
   128	\EXP{\VAR{wrap}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
   129	and \EXP{\VAR{id}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T},
   130	the variable declaration \EXP{a\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket = \VAR{wrap}(3)}
   131	instantiates \VAR{wrap} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, which the expected type fixes,
   132	and coerces the numeral, while \EXP{b\COLON\mathbb{Z}64 = \VAR{id}(3)}
   133	instantiates \VAR{id} at the numeral's own type (\secref{literals}) and coerces
   134	the result.
   135	
   136	\emph{Dispatch.}
   137	The call, with the coercions of its instance inserted, dispatches at run time
   138	as \secref{resolving-overloading} describes, by subtyping and without further
   139	coercion, to the most specific declaration applicable to the converted values.

   162	\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
   163	\seclabel{numeral-default}
   164	
   165	A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
   166	number types (\secref{literals}).
   167	Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
   168	$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
   169	taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
   170	a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
   171	value does not fit in the narrower type.
   172	This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
   173	to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
   174	and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.

   176	\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
   177	type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and

   179	instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
   180	values.
   181	
   182	The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
   183	Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
   184	call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
   185	is a static error.
   186

   188	\begin{itemize}
   189	\item the static arguments of a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator
   190	parameter (\secref{boolparams}, \secref{dimunitparams}, \secref{opr-ident});
   191	\item a static parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes,
   192	such as a type parameter that only the return type mentions, as its whole type,

   194	(\secref{reduction-expr}); whether inference may give such a parameter

   199	elements would satisfy the bounds of the parameter; under the rule above such

   205	juxtaposition, as \EXP{f\;x};
   206	\item the static arguments of an object with static parameters that is named
   207	without a call, which a program writes (\secref{where-clauses});
   208	\item the inference over a whole program of the types that declarations elide

   217	below.
   218	Neither implementation infers a \KWD{bool} parameter yet: the compiled type
   219	checker refuses by name to infer a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim} or \KWD{unit}
   220	parameter, and the interpreter does not unify a \KWD{bool} one (rows~21
   221	and~307 of the revival's gap ledger).
   222	The example of \secref{boolparams}, a coercion whose \KWD{bool} parameter only
   223	its parameter type mentions, can be applied only if its argument fixes that
   224	parameter.}
   225	
   226	\note{ \begin{itemize}
   227	 \item

   230	 to disambiguate, but you can't do that without using inference, which
   231	 requires knowing how the variable of unknown type is used.
   232	\item Type Inference (Dan's email titled ``Comments on a first reading of the spec'' on 06/05/07)

  1101	The full reasoning is in
  1102	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-ranges/decision-record.md}
  1103	in the revival's repository.
  1104	\item[Effect] A program writes a range over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} where it wrote
  1105	one over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} or
  1106	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, and widens its elements where it needs a wider counter; a
  1107	range over another integer type is refused. Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter may
  1108	be a component of a range, which this change left open, is settled by
  1109	\secref{revival-inference}: it converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an integer
  1110	numeral does.
  1111	\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/ranges.tex},
  1112	lines 42--44:
  1545	\EXP{\KWD{trait}\:\mathbb{Q}\;\KWD{extends}\:\TYP{Number}}.
  1546	\item[Route C] By the revival's reading, not measured, the same under route~C.
  1547	\end{description}
  1548	
  1549	\subsection{The inference of a call's static arguments}
  1550	\seclabel{revival-inference}
  1551	
  1552	\begin{description}
  1553	\item[Affected sections] \chapref{type-inference}; \secref{ranges};
  1554	\secref{basic-integers}; \secref{revival-ranges}; \secref{revival-notrevised}.
  1555	\item[Change] \chapref{type-inference}, which held a heading and two draft
  1556	notes, states how the static arguments of a call that does not write them are
  1557	inferred, for type parameters and for \KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters.
  1558	The declaration is chosen first, as \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses it, a
  1559	declaration with static parameters being applicable to a call if some instance
  1560	of it within its bounds is, and compared on the parameter types it declares.
  1561	Its static arguments are then inferred: a type, \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
  1562	parameter that a parameter type mentions inside another type is fixed by the
  1563	argument, and a type parameter that the return type mentions inside another
  1564	type by the expected type; a type parameter that
  1565	is the whole type of parameters takes the narrowest type that their arguments
  1566	are substitutable for, which for number arguments is the narrowest type into
  1567	which every one of them converts, and otherwise the union of their types; every
  1568	argument is admitted by substitutability, the coercions the instance needs are
  1569	inserted statically, and the converted call dispatches by subtyping.
  1570	A call written by tight juxtaposition, as a method invocation or as an operator
  1571	application, has an expected type in the contexts the chapter lists, a variable
  1572	or field declaration and an assignment to a variable among them, and is
  1573	inferred again without it when its result then converts.
  1574	A numeral whose conversions tie is read as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a
  1575	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} by its value; any other tie among
  1576	declarations applicable only with coercion is a static error.
  1577	The chapter lists what it does not yet describe, the static arguments of a
  1578	\KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator parameter among them, keeps the
  1579	second of the two draft notes, and has three boxes: on the Working Draft, the
  1580	bound it assumes and the passages it leaves to the revision of the overloading
  1581	chapters; on the interpreter; and on a type parameter that only the return
  1582	type mentions and on the \KWD{bool} parameters that neither implementation
  1583	infers.
  1584	The ranges section says that a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
  1585	component converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an integer numeral does, with a
  1586	box.
  1587	The box in \secref{basic-integers} says that a generic call over two different
  1588	integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into by the rule of
  1589	\chapref{type-inference}.
  1590	\secref{revival-notrevised} says that the rule is written and names the passages
  1591	the chapter leaves unrevised, and it and the effect of \secref{revival-ranges}
  1592	say that the question of a \KWD{nat} parameter in a range is settled.
  1593	\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A.
  1594	The revival decided on 26~September 2026 that a generic call over two different
  1595	integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into, by a rule
  1596	written into this chapter; on 27~September 2026 that the compiled type checker
  1597	infers static arguments with coercion and keeps the expected type at a call
  1598	written as \EXP{f(x)}, with a retry without it so that a coercion of the result
  1599	still applies, and that the chapter is written with it; and on 28~September
  1600	2026 that a coercion makes a call possible and never changes which declaration
  1601	runs when one is applicable without it, the declaration chosen being then
  1602	instantiated by that rule, that a numeral whose conversions tie is read as a
  1603	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and that a \KWD{nat} parameter used as a value converts to
  1604	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as a numeral does.
  1605	\chapref{multiple-dispatch}, \secref{idn-ref} and \secref{dotted-method-calls}
  1606	said that static arguments are inferred as \chapref{type-inference} describes,
  1607	and it described nothing; once the compiled type checker infers them by a rule
  1608	the text does not state, the text and the implementation disagree, so the
  1609	chapter states the rule that the checker builds, and no more.
  1610	The order, a declaration chosen and then instantiated, is that of
  1611	\secref{resolving-coercion}, read on the parameter types that declarations
  1612	declare, as the type group's paper of 2011 reads a declaration with static
  1613	parameters: it ``is applicable to a type if and only if at least one of its
  1614	instances is'' (\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/setup.tick}, lines 396--397, in the
  1615	revival's repository).
  1616	The numeral's default is what the interpreter did before this change, giving
  1617	a numeral the narrowest of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
  1618	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} that holds its value, \library\ declaring their numeral type
  1619	below \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}; the compiled path, whose library declares its
  1620	numeral type beside \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and excluding it, took one of the
  1621	declarations that a numeral left tied, and not always the same one (row~391 of
  1622	the revival's gap ledger).
  1623	It is also the Java programming language's type for an integer literal.
  1624	The compiled type checker gives a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
  1625	value the type of a numeral, and the interpreter makes it a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
  1626	so an \KWD{int} parameter is read as a \KWD{nat} parameter is; on the Java
  1627	Virtual Machine the length and the indices of an array are 32-bit integers.
  1628	The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) gives the coercion relation,
  1629	the coercion of a generic type and the valid instantiations of a quantified
  1630	type (\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
  1631	938--947, 393--400 and 771--789, in the revival's repository) and never uses
  1632	the word ``infer''; the type group's paper leaves the run-time inference of the
  1633	static arguments of a dispatched declaration ``beyond the scope of this paper''
  1634	(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 118--129).
  1635	The full reasoning is in
  1636	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-inference/decision-record.md}
  1637	in the revival's repository.
  1638	\item[Effect] A generic call over two different integer types, or over a number
  1639	type and a numeral, need not write its static argument, and the interim rule
  1640	of the effect of \secref{revival-numbers} ends.

  1642	as \EXP{f(x)} mentions inside another type, and a call whose result the
  1643	declared type converts is accepted as before.
  1644	Where the conversions of a numeral tie, the \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} declaration or
  1645	instance is taken; where another argument's conversions tie, the call is a

1	# Decision record: the type-inference chapter (rung T, climb batch N)
     2	
     3	This is the decision record the S1 form asks for (`explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-26, S1): each revised passage, the original, the new text, why it changed, and the way back. Appendix I's entry "The inference of a call's static arguments" (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1549-1711`, `\seclabel{revival-inference}`) names this file. The base is `bce66f1fa`. "The Working Draft of February 2011" is the unrevised copy under `Specification-1.0-frozen/` (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, the first of the batch-5 answers). `Specification/basic/inference.tex` on the base equals `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/inference.tex` byte for byte (`diff`, no output), so its base lines are the frozen copy's lines; `ranges.tex`, `basic-integers.tex` and `changes.tex` were revised by the revival before this rung, and their base lines are given as base lines.
     4	
     5	The decisions this rung carries out, quoted from POSITIONS.md:
     6	- **The numerics plans**, 2026-09-27, the synthesis's decision 3, "Agreed." (19:30 UTC): "the checker infers a static argument with coercion (answer 8's promotion rule, the narrowest type every number argument converts into, is its number case) and keeps the expected type at a call written `f(x)` with a retry without it, so that a binding's coercion still applies; walk does the same at dispatch; [...] the specification's type-inference chapter is written in the S1 form and lands only with the checker rung."
     7	- **The two decisions of the conversion judgement**, 2026-09-28, "Both recommendations for batch N accepted." (19:06 UTC), decision 1: "a conversion is applied to make a call possible and never changes which declaration runs when one already fits; declarations are chosen by the coercion chapter's order, applicability and specificity taken on declared, quantified domains as answer 9 words them (a generic declaration fits when some instance within its bound fits); the chosen declaration is then instantiated by answer 8's promotion, its coercions inserted statically, and the rewritten call dispatches on the converted values; a numeral whose candidate types are incomparable reads as `ZZ32` (`ZZ64` or `ZZ` by magnitude), stated once in the inference chapter." The judgement's section 5 gives this rung "the instantiation step as the second step after the coercion chapter's resolution, in the words of section 1, with the static insertion of the instance's coercions, the dispatch on converted values, the numeral default once, and a callout that walk applies the same rule from run-time types" (`explorations/reviews/conversion-overloading-judgement.md:143-153`).
     8	- **Answer 8**, 2026-09-26: "A generic call or range over mixed widths infers the narrowest type both sides coerce into, a promotion rule written into the specification's empty inference chapter."
     9	- **A size used as a value**, 2026-09-28, PLAN item 25, "Option 1, go ahead." (19:17 UTC): "A size used as a value converts to `ZZ32` as a numeral does. [...] Batch N carries it: rung I converts it as a numeral, rung T writes it into the ranges section (row 485)."
    10	- **Q1 = (1)**, the conversion judgement's section 4, taken at its default and listed for Pavol's review with the judgement's other defaults (the batch record, section 1; this rung's section, "The answers this rung follows").
    11	
    12	Rung I builds the rule in the compiled checker beside this rung and is not in this rung's tree; section 6 lists every statement the chapter makes that the gather checks against I's landed tests. The chapter lands only if I lands (the manifest entry's `landsOnlyWith`).
    13	
    14	## 1. The list
    15	
    16	The list, written before any edit and committed first (`bcd9f07df`), is `probes/list.txt`: seven revisions (R1 to R7) and twenty-four passages left (L1 to L24), each with the source that settles it; one passage left (L25) and one defect (M1) were found after it, and one more passage (L26) by the first skeptic, all in section 4. It starts from evidence B's section 1.2 (`explorations/reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/evidence-B.md:47-60`), every passage of which is in it (`overloading.tex:170-175`, `:202-207`, `:291-296`, `:136-138` as L1; `inference.tex` as R1; `components/type-inference.tex:15-18` as L13; `var-ref.tex:35-40` and `method-invocation.tex:49-52` as L9; the callout as R3; `trait-parameters.tex:478-485` as L15; `reductions.tex:27-44` with `defining-generators.tex` as L14), and adds what a grep for `type-inference` (17 hits), `infer` (51) and the brief's other terms found: the union types' sentence (L11), the type ascription's (L10), the bottom type's (L12), the passages on elided declaration types (L22), the team's commented or noted text (L23), the Appendix I sentences (R4 to R6, L19, L20), the implicit bound and the naked-Any rule (L2, L3), and the coercion chapter's passages (L4 to L8).
    17	
    18	## 2. What the revision states, and what it does not
    19	
    20	The chapter (`Specification/basic/inference.tex:15-236`) states, for a call of a function, a method, an operator or a constructor whose declaration has static parameters and whose static arguments are not written, and for type parameters and `nat` and `int` parameters only (the scope sentence, `:19-25`, since the repair round):
    21	- **Choice** (`:60-69`): the declaration is chosen as `\secref{resolving-coercion}` describes (cited, not restated); a declaration with static parameters is applicable, with or without coercion, if some instance within its bounds is; declarations are compared on their declared parameter types, quantified over the instances their bounds allow, not on an inferred instance; so a coercion never changes which declaration is chosen when one applies without it.
    22	- **Instantiation** (`:71-106`): a type, `nat` or `int` parameter mentioned inside a parameter type is fixed by that argument by subtyping (`:75-79`); a type parameter mentioned inside the declared return type is fixed by the expected type too (`:80-82`); a type parameter that is the whole type of parameters takes, among its arguments' types and the types they can be coerced to, the narrowest under `⪯` that every argument is substitutable for and its bounds permit; for number arguments the narrowest type every one converts into (ZZ64 for ZZ32 with ZZ64, and for ZZ32 with NN32); otherwise, unless the numeral rule settles the tie, the union of the arguments' types if the bounds permit, with no conversion; every argument admitted by substitutability against the instance's parameter types, coerced where it is not a subtype; the coercions inserted statically.
    23	- **The expected type** (`:108-134`): the contexts that give one (`:109-116`: the right-hand side of a variable or field declaration that declares its type, the right-hand side of an assignment to a variable whose type is declared, a functional's body against its declared return type, a block's last expression where no local declaration precedes it, both branches of an `if` with `else`); used at a call written by tight juxtaposition `f(x)`, a method invocation or an operator application; the instance's return type must be a subtype of it, and failing that the inference runs again without it and the call is accepted only if the result is a subtype of or coerces to the expected type, the result then coerced. Two examples: `a: List[\ZZ64\] = wrap(3)` (T fixed by the expected type, the numeral coerced) and `b: ZZ64 = id(3)` (the numeral's own type, the result coerced).
    24	- **Dispatch** (`:136-139`), in the judgement's words: the converted call dispatches at run time by subtyping, without further coercion, to the most specific declaration applicable to the converted values. One example (`:141-148`): `op(z, w)` with `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` and `op(a: Any, b: Any)` chooses the generic declaration, instantiates it at ZZ64 and coerces `z` (`OpAnyZW`'s shape).
    25	- **A numeral whose conversions tie** (`:162-185`, `\seclabel{numeral-default}`), once: read as ZZ32, or ZZ64 or ZZ by its value, in either step; two examples (`g(0)` over `g(x: NN32)` and `g(x: ZZ32)` takes the second; a type parameter only numerals fix, bounded so that ZZ32 and NN32 satisfy its bounds and the numeral's type does not, takes ZZ32); the rule ranks nothing else, and a non-numeral argument that leaves declarations applicable only with coercion tied makes the call a static error.
    26	- **What it does not yet describe** (`:187-210`): the static arguments of a `bool`, `dim`, `unit` or operator parameter (`:189-190`, since the repair round); a static parameter nothing fixes (a result-only type parameter, a reduction's element type), with the BottomType question left open; whether an argument that fixes a parameter through a structure may be converted; an expected type in any other context (an argument, an expression after a local declaration, an `if` without `else`, `typecase`, a `for` body, loose juxtaposition `f x`); a generic object named without a call; whole-program inference of elided types.

== cc 417-432
We say that a type $T$ is \emph{substitutable} for type $U$, and we
write $T \substitutable U$, if $T$ is a subtype of $U$ or $T$ can be
coerced to $U$; that is,
\[
T \substitutable U \iff T \Ovrsubtype U \logicor T \coercesto U.
\]

Note that $\substitutable$ need not be transitive.  This is a result
of the fact that coercion does not chain.
However, if $T$ is substitutable for $U$ then so are $T$'s subtypes;
that is, $A \Ovrsubtype T \logicand T \substitutable U \implies A
\substitutable U$.

A declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{applicable with coercion} to a
call $\f(\Cs)$ if the call is in the scope of the declaration and
$\Cs \substitutable \Ps$.

\section{Coercion Resolution}
\seclabel{resolving-coercion}
For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a
declaration that is applicable without coercion.  If so, the most
specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are
explicitly added to the functional call.  If more than one coercion is
possible then the coercion that yields the most specific type is
chosen.  \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
\chapref{overloaded-declarations} describe overloading rules for the
declarations of coercions and overloaded functionals that guarantee
there exists always a most specific coercion when two or more are possible.

We first define a notion of more specific types in the presence of coercion.

#!/bin/bash
# run-both.sh <probe.fss>... : each probe under walk and compiled (against the compiler library), at FORTRESS_THREADS=1, on this worktree (the worker's run-both.sh, skeptic's copy)
W=/home/user/fortress-specinfer
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH FORTRESS_HOME=$W TMPDIR=$W/tmp FORTRESS_THREADS=1
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$W/tmp"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
echo "# machine: nproc $(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=1; tree $(git -C $W rev-parse --short HEAD)$(git -C $W diff --quiet -- ProjectFortress Library || echo '+working-tree-edits')"
for p in "$@"; do
  d=$(dirname $p); f=$(basename $p)
  echo "=== $f walk"
  ( cd $d && timeout 300 $W/bin/fortress $f 2>&1 | grep -v '^\s*at ' | head -30 ; echo "rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}" )
  echo "=== $f compile"
  ( cd $d && timeout 300 $W/bin/fortress compile $f 2>&1 | head -30 ; echo "rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}" )
  echo "=== $f compiled run"
  ( cd $d && timeout 300 $W/bin/fortress run ${f%.fss} 2>&1 | grep -v '^\s*at ' | head -30 ; echo "rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}" )
done

  /**
   * Given a static parameters, returns a static arg containing a fresh

  def makeInferenceArg(sparam: StaticParam): StaticArg = sparam.getKind match {
    case _: KindType => 
      NF.makeTypeArg(NU.getSpan(sparam), NF.make_InferenceVarType(NU.getSpan(sparam)),
                     sparam.isLifted)
    case _: KindInt => makeSizeInferenceArg(sparam)
    case _: KindBool => unsupportedKindError(sparam, "bool")
    case _: KindDim => unsupportedKindError(sparam, "dim")
    case _: KindOp => NF.makeOpArg(NU.getSpan(sparam),
                      NF.make_InferenceVarOp(NU.getSpan(sparam)),
                      sparam.isLifted) // DRC- opArgs also lifted?
    case _: KindUnit => unsupportedKindError(sparam, "unit")
    case _: KindNat => makeSizeInferenceArg(sparam)
    case _ => bug("unexpected kind of static parameter")
  }

  private def makeSizeInferenceArg(sparam: StaticParam): StaticArg =
    NF.makeIntArg(NU.getSpan(sparam), NF.make_InferenceVarInt(NU.getSpan(sparam)),
                  sparam.isLifted)

  private def unsupportedKindError(sparam: StaticParam, kind: String): StaticArg =
    throw TypeError.make("Static argument inference for the " + kind + " static parameter " +
